name: Treaty with the Iowa, 1837
nations: Iowa (Ioway) Nation, today the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska and the Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma
promises: Article 1: the Iowa ceded all their right and interest in the land ceded by the treaty of July 15, 1830 (Prairie du Chien) that they might claim under its second article.
Article 2: the United States would pay $2,500 in horses, goods and presents when they signed.
Article 3: the United States would pay the costs of the negotiation and the delegates' travel.

breaches.what: The Commission had found that the Iowa held an undivided one-fourth interest in most of Royce Cession 151 and that their interest in the western Iowa part passed to the United States under this treaty. The Iowa claim (Docket 138) was then settled by compromise for a stipulated net judgment, which the Commission approved.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Findings of Fact in the Matter of the Compromise Settlement of Dockets 138 and 339 (March 22, 1965)

source.title: Iowa Tribe v. United States, Dockets 138 and 339, Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement (1965)
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

landTaken: Royce Areas 151 and 152, the 1830 Prairie du Chien cession, in which the Iowa interest was one of four (Docket 138 findings, 1965).
compensation: $2,500 in goods at signing (treaty text). The 1965 stipulation reads as a net judgment of $1,372,267.50 for the Iowa tribes, with $150,000 withheld pending the Yankton Sioux claim in Docket 332-A (see openQuestions).
today: The settlement was a compromise, not a finding that the 1837 price was unconscionable. The 1830 treaty itself is kappler-313.

openQuestions: The scan of the stipulation renders the judgment as '$1,372,267 .SO' once and '$1,312,267 .SO' once; the reading $1,372,267.50 should be checked against a clean copy.
The Commission dates the passing of title to February 16, 1838, the ratification date; OSU gives the proclamation as February 21, 1838.
